title: Access keys: where they never go
promise: You'll get your keys out of where they shouldn't be, keep them in one safe place, and know what to do in the ten minutes after leaking one. By the end you'll have done the full sweep and rotated one key.
why: A student uploaded his project to GitHub to show a client. Inside a configuration file was his OpenAI key, typed in by hand because «it was only for testing». In nine hours he had $340 of usage. The bots crawling GitHub for keys don't take days: they take minutes. It wasn't bad luck and it wasn't an attack aimed at him. It was the normal workings of the internet applied to a file that should never have left his computer.

theory.title: What a key is and why it's worth money
theory.text: An access key, what you'll see called an API key, is a password you give a program so it can act on your behalf in another service. It isn't your personal password: it's a permission anyone holding it can use, from anywhere, without warning you. There's no second check, no notification email, no code to your phone. Whoever has it, is you. And on pay-per-use services, being you means spending your money. That's the important difference from an ordinary password: a stolen password is stolen from you; a stolen key gets used, and the charge lands all the same.
theory.analogy: It's a copy of the warehouse key with your name on the invoice. It doesn't matter who opens it: whatever they take, you pay for, and nobody calls to ask whether it was you going in at four in the morning.
theory.example: $340 in nine hours, with the key in a file inside a public repository. No warning at all until the charge email arrived.

theory.title: The four places they always end up
theory.text: Keys almost always leak by the same four routes, and none of them is sophisticated. First, typed inside a project file that later gets pushed to GitHub. Second, pasted into a chat with an AI to ask for help with an error, with the key inside the message. Third, in a screenshot sent over WhatsApp or put into a tutorial. And fourth, in an error message copied verbatim into a forum, because many errors include the full request. In all four the pattern is the same: the key travels attached to something else, and you were looking at the something else.
theory.example: «I copied the whole error so people could help me» is leak route number three, and the one fewest people see coming.
theory.analogy: Keys always end up in the same four places: in the lock, under the mat, in the pocket of a coat you no longer wear, and lent to someone who doesn't remember. It doesn't take a sophisticated burglar.

theory.title: The only place they go: environment variables
theory.text: The answer isn't hiding them better inside the project: it's them not being inside it at all. Keys go in environment variables, which is a separate place the program reads them from when it starts. In a local project that means a file called dot env, which never gets uploaded because it's listed in the exclusions file. On Vercel, Netlify or any hosting, it's a settings screen where you paste them and that's that. In n8n or Make, it's the credentials section, which stores them encrypted and shows them as dots. The rule is one line: if a key appears written in a file you can open in a text editor and read, it's in the wrong place.
theory.example: Bad: a line in the code with the key typed in. Good: the line reads a variable, and that variable's value lives in the settings panel, outside the project.
theory.analogy: You don't hide money better inside the house: you take it to the bank. It isn't a cleverer hiding place, it's a different place, and the house stops having it.

theory.title: One key per place, with the minimum permission
theory.text: Two habits that cost a minute and are worth a great deal. First: a different key for every place you use it. One for your computer, another for what's published, another for each workflow. That way, if one leaks, you revoke that one and everything else carries on working, instead of having to reconnect the lot at once under pressure. Second: give the minimum permission. Many services let you create read-only keys, or ones limited to one part. If your setup only reads, the key has no business being able to delete. And name them when you create them, because a list of eight keys called «key1» is impossible to manage the day you're in a hurry.
theory.example: «nuria-laptop», «n8n-reminders», «published-site». When the odd-usage warning fires, you know which to revoke without touching the other two.
theory.analogy: The front-door key doesn't open your flat, and the mailbox key opens nothing else. Lose one and you change one lock, not all of them.

theory.title: The ten minutes after leaking one
theory.text: It's going to happen, and what matters is the reaction. The right order is this and the order matters. First: revoke the key on the service's website, the revoke or delete button. Not change it, revoke it. Second: create a new one and put it where it belongs, in the environment variable. Third: look at the last few hours' usage in case it's already been used. And fourth, the one almost everyone skips: if it was in a git repository, deleting it from the file doesn't delete it from the history. It's still there, recoverable, forever. That's why the first step is to revoke and not to delete the file: as long as the key is revoked, it doesn't matter who finds it.
theory.example: Deleting the key and making a commit saying «removed the key» is worse than doing nothing: it doesn't take it out of the history and it flags where it was.
theory.analogy: When you lose your card, you call to cancel it first and search the house afterwards. The other way round, you can spend two hours searching while someone is using it.

theory.title: What you don't paste into an AI
theory.text: When you ask an AI for help with an error, it's very easy to paste more than you meant to. Before pressing send, scan the text for four things: long strings of letters and numbers starting with sk-, api-, ghp- or similar; internal addresses from your company; people's data with names attached; and the contents of configuration files. Replacing them with something like KEY-REMOVED takes nothing away from the help you'll get: for diagnosing an error, the key's value contributes nothing. What contributes is the message and the three-digit code.
theory.example: «401 error with key sk-proj-abc123...» → «401 error with key KEY-REMOVED». The help is exactly the same.
theory.analogy: Showing a photo of the living room to ask about the wall colour, with a bank statement visible on the table. The photo was of the wall; what's visible is everything else.

tasks.title: Take an inventory of your keys
tasks.where: In a text file, and on your services' websites
tasks.action: Write the list of every service where you have a key created: OpenAI, Anthropic, n8n, GitHub, the hosting, whatever. Next to each, put where that key currently sits, honestly. If it's typed into a project file, write that down. This list doesn't contain the keys themselves, only the names and the places.
tasks.expect: A list of between three and eight services. The usual surprise is finding keys created months ago for a test and still active.
tasks.stuck: To find them, go into each service and look for the API keys section. You'll see how many you have and when each was last used. Revoke any that haven't been used in months right now: it's the most profitable tidy-up in the block.
tasks.prompt:
Help me inventory my keys, which is the thing nobody has until they need it.

SERVICES I USE: [OpenAI, Anthropic, n8n, GitHub, hosting, whatever]
WHERE I THINK THEY'RE PLUGGED IN: [my computer, a flow, the published site…]

Build me a table with one row per key and these columns: SERVICE / WHAT I USE IT FOR / WHERE IT'S PLUGGED IN RIGHT NOW / WHAT HAPPENS IF IT LEAKS / WHERE IT GETS REVOKED (exact web address).

Write the leak column concretely, with money where there is money: "someone can spend on my account with no cap" says more than "high risk". And add at the end the services I probably have and haven't named, based on what I've told you — the forgotten ones are exactly the ones lying around.

tasks.title: Search for keys where they shouldn't be
tasks.action: Open your project folder and use the search to find suspicious text. In Windows search or Spotlight, search inside files for «sk-», «api_key», «apikey», «token» and «password». Also look at the configuration files and any notes files where you've been jotting things down. Note every place you find a key typed in.
tasks.expect: With luck, zero results. What's normal is finding one or two, almost always in a test file from the first few days.
tasks.stuck: If you use git, look at the history too: in GitHub Desktop, the History tab, and go back through old commits looking for configuration files. A key can be out of today's project and still inside yesterday's history.
tasks.prompt:
Help me hunt for keys written where they shouldn't be, in my own project.

SYSTEM: [Windows / Mac / Linux]
WHAT'S IN MY FOLDER: [a website, exported flows, sheets, scripts…]
SERVICES I USE: [LIST]

Tell me one, what exact strings to search for: the prefixes my services' keys start with, and the words that usually sit next to them (api_key, token, password, secret, bearer). Two, how to search INSIDE file contents on my system, with the exact steps. Three, which places to check that aren't code files: exported flows, screenshots, notes, terminal history.

Warn me about false positives so I don't panic over nothing. And tell me what to do if I find a key in something I've already pushed online, because the order matters there.

tasks.title: Move them out to environment variables
tasks.where: In your project and on your hosting
tasks.action: For every key you found typed in: create or open the «.env» file in your project's root and put a line in it with the name and the value. Check that «.env» is listed in the «.gitignore» file; if that file doesn't exist, create it and write .env inside. In the code, replace the typed key with a read of that variable. And if the project is published, paste the same value into your hosting's environment variables screen.
tasks.expect: No key typed into any file in the project. Check in GitHub Desktop that the «.env» file doesn't appear in the changes list: if it does, the .gitignore isn't right and you'd upload it again.
tasks.stuck: If you don't know how a variable is read in your case, ask the AI, saying which language or tool you use, but without pasting it the key. And if your setup is n8n or Make, this is even easier: use the tool's own credentials section, which already stores them encrypted.
tasks.prompt:
Help me get my keys out of the code and into environment variables.

PROJECT TYPE: [website, Python script, n8n flow, something else]
WHERE THE KEY IS NOW: [paste the line, with the key MASKED]
WHERE IT WILL RUN: [my computer / a server / Vercel / n8n cloud]

Tell me: one, which file I create and what goes inside, with the exact naming format for the variable. Two, how I change the line of code to read from there. Three, which file I have to add to .gitignore, and why that isn't enough if the key was already pushed. Four, how those same variables get set where it'll be published, which is not the same as on my machine.

Finish by telling me how to check it works: what I should see if it reads the variable correctly, and what error I'll get if it can't find it, so I recognise it when it shows up.

tasks.title: Rehearse revoking a key
tasks.where: On one of your services' websites
tasks.action: This is a drill, like the one in lesson 37. Take a key you use and revoke it for real: go into the service, revoke it, create a new one, and put it in place. Time it. What you're measuring is how long it would take you the day one leaks, and along the way you discover how many places had to be updated, which is almost always more than you thought.
tasks.expect: Everything working again and a time noted down. Note also how many places you had to paste the new key into: that number tells you whether separate keys per place would suit you.
tasks.stuck: If revoking it breaks three things at once and takes you half an hour, you've just discovered why one key per place is worth having. Create them separately now while you're at it.
tasks.prompt:
I'm running a drill: revoking a real key and putting a new one in, to find out how long it takes and what breaks.

SERVICE: [WHICH]
WHERE THAT KEY IS PLUGGED IN: [list every place you can think of]
WHAT STOPS MEANWHILE: [nothing / a flow / the website]

Write me the drill in order, with the name of each button:
1. Where it gets revoked in that service, exactly.
2. Where the new one is created and which permissions I give it — the minimum.
3. Every place it has to be pasted, in the order that leaves the service down for the least time.
4. How I check everything is working again, place by place.

Also tell me which place people always forget and discover three days later. I'm going to time it: tell me how long it should take so I know whether I'm on track.

tasks.title: Set the spending limit, if you haven't already
tasks.action: This is the net that catches you if everything above fails. If you did it in lesson 38, review it. If not, go into each service's billing section and set a hard monthly limit and a warning at half. This is the only measure that turns a $340 leak into a $35 one.
tasks.expect: A limit and a warning set on each service, with the email address you actually read.
tasks.stuck: If a service doesn't allow a hard limit, compensate elsewhere: use a prepaid card with a small balance or check the usage weekly. And keep a close eye on that account, because it's the one that can hurt you.
tasks.prompt:
Help me set a spending cap on every pay-per-use service, which is the net that saves me if a key leaks.

SERVICES I PAY BY USAGE: [LIST]
WHAT I SPEND A MONTH: [APPROXIMATE]
WORST THING THAT COULD HAPPEN: [a flow stops / an enormous bill]

For each service: where the limits section is, with the screen name, which two different things I set (the alert and the hard cap), and what number goes in each based on my spend.

Explain the difference between the alert and the cap, because plenty of people set only the alert and think they're protected. And tell me exactly what happens when the cap is hit: what error my flows get, and whether it clears itself next month or I have to go and change something.

tasks.title: Write your leak protocol
tasks.action: Four lines written to be read with your pulse racing: where each key is revoked (the exact web address for each service), where the new one has to be pasted, where you check the usage, and the reminder that deleting the file doesn't remove it from git history. Save it alongside the course's other files.
tasks.expect: Four lines with concrete links. On the day it happens you won't be in a state to go hunting for which menu the revoke button was in.
tasks.stuck: If you think it won't happen to you, bear in mind the commonest route isn't a big careless mistake: it's pasting a long error message into a chat without looking at what was inside it. It's a matter of time.
tasks.prompt:
Help me write my leak protocol, to read with my pulse racing.

MY SERVICES AND WHERE EACH KEY GETS REVOKED: [PASTE YOUR INVENTORY]
WHERE EACH KEY IS PLUGGED IN: [LIST]

Write me four lines, in the imperative, no explanations, in the correct order of action. The first has to be revoke, not search: I want that order written down, because in a panic people do it the other way round.

Underneath, two more lines: what I check to find out whether the key was actually used (where each service's usage history lives), and who I notify if the data involved belonged to someone else. All of it fits on half a screen: if it doesn't fit, it won't get read on the day it's needed.

matters: That a key is permission to act on your behalf and spend your money, with no second check.
That they leak by four routes and the commonest is pasting a long error into a chat.
That they go in environment variables, outside any project file.
That the first thing on a leak is to revoke, not delete: deleting the file doesn't take it out of the history.
ignore: Professional secret managers. Environment variables and the tool's credentials will serve you.
Encrypting the keys yourself. The right place already stores them properly.
Rotating them monthly out of habit. Better few, well placed, and with a spending cap.
canDo: Know how many live keys you have and where each one is.
Get them out of project files and into environment variables.
Revoke and replace a key in minutes, because you've rehearsed it.
Bound the damage of a leak with a spending limit.
cantDo: Get back money already spent with a leaked key.
Remove a key from git history by deleting the file.
Find out it's being used if you have no usage warnings.
Eliminate the risk entirely: only reduce it and react fast.
words: Permission for a program to act on your behalf in another service. Whoever has it, is you.
The separate place a key lives, outside the project's files.
The local file those variables go in. It never gets uploaded: it's in the .gitignore.
Cancelling a key so it stops working. The first thing you do about a leak.
Giving each key only what it needs. If your setup only reads, the key shouldn't be able to delete.
next: The keys are where they should be. In lesson 41 you go to what causes the most legal trouble: other people's data that you put into these tools, and what can go in and what can't.
